public_rationale: The claim is graded over the 26 months named in the title: from the March 10, 2022 essay to the post date of June 1, 2024. It is read as saying that leading developers had not resolved the problems the post names, chiefly unreliability and hallucinations. The evidence supports this narrower reading. In March 2023, OpenAI said GPT-4 'still is not fully reliable' and 'hallucinates' facts (e1). In a post published May 30, 2024, Google said that 'odd, inaccurate or unhelpful' AI Overviews 'certainly did show up' (e2). In May 2024, a Stanford study found that legal AI tools whose providers claimed they avoid hallucinations still produced incorrect information more than 17% of the time (Lexis+ AI, Ask Practical Law AI) and more than 34% of the time (Westlaw AI-Assisted Research) (e3). OpenAI also reported progress: GPT-4 scored 40% higher than GPT-3.5 on its internal factuality evaluations, and it still called hallucinations 'a real issue' (e4). That is a reduction, not a resolution. The post's claims that alignment is 'no closer' and that the technology is 'exactly as incorrigible' are not graded here.
limitations: 'What ails their AI' is not defined in the sentence; the grade uses the problems the post names, mainly hallucinations and reliability.
None of the cited evidence addresses toxicity, which the post also names.

The evidence includes some measures of improvement, such as OpenAI's internal factuality score (e4) and Stanford's finding that the legal tools made fewer errors than GPT-4 (e3). It does not track how much the problems changed across the whole period or across all leading systems.
The grade does not cover the stronger claims that there was no progress or that alignment is no closer. The evidence of progress (e4) would complicate those claims.
Google said AI Overviews generally do not 'hallucinate' in the way other LLM products might. Its admission (e2) is about inaccurate answers, not hallucination as such.

statement.excerpt: The ridicule is of me; the failure is of the lords of deep learning to resolve what ails their AI.

from_speaker: the failure is of the lords of deep learning
to resolve what ails their AI
26 months later (since the 'Deep Learning is Hitting a Wall' essay)
toxicity and hallucinations are still with us
our_interpretation: 'What ails their AI' is read from the post's own list: unreliability, hallucinations and toxicity in leading deep-learning systems such as large language models.

'Failure to resolve' is read as: by the post date, leading developers had not eliminated these problems, so their flagship systems still made confident factual errors. Progress or partial reductions do not count as resolution.
The separate claim that we are 'no closer' on alignment is not graded here. Only the narrower claim that the problems remained unresolved is graded.
The target period runs from the March 2022 essay to the post date, 2024-06-01.
criteria.support_condition: Developer statements or independent evaluations from the period showing that leading deep-learning systems still hallucinated or were unreliable as of mid-2024.
criteria.contradiction_condition: Credible evidence that by June 2024 leading developers had effectively eliminated hallucinations and unreliability in their flagship systems, such as evaluations showing near-zero factual error rates in normal use.

evidence.excerpt: Despite its capabilities, GPT‑4 has similar limitations as earlier GPT models. Most importantly, it still is not fully reliable (it “hallucinates” facts and makes reasoning errors).
evidence.explanation: The leading lab says its flagship model, released within the period, still hallucinates and is not fully reliable.

evidence.excerpt: But some odd, inaccurate or unhelpful AI Overviews certainly did show up.
evidence.locator: section About those odd results, paragraph 3
evidence.explanation: Days before the post, Google admitted its new AI search feature gave inaccurate answers at launch. This shows reliability problems were still present.

evidence.excerpt: even these bespoke legal AI tools still hallucinate an alarming amount of the time: the Lexis+ AI and Ask Practical Law AI systems produced incorrect information more than 17% of the time, while Westlaw’s AI-Assisted Research hallucinated more than 34% of the time.
evidence.locator: section AI-Driven Legal Research Tools Still Hallucinate, paragraph 1
evidence.explanation: In May 2024, an independent test found that commercial tools built on LLMs and marketed as hallucination-free still hallucinated often.

evidence.excerpt: While still a real issue, GPT‑4 significantly reduces hallucinations relative to previous models (which have themselves been improving with each iteration).
evidence.explanation: This shows real progress in reducing hallucinations during the period. It does not show they were resolved; the same passage calls them 'still a real issue'.
